Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 527 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Header title 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 527 is located in north-west Alberta, covering an area of 6767 km2. The unit is 
bordered by the 25th base line (northern boundary of Township 96) to the north, the Peace River to the east, 
Highway 684 and Highway 35 to the southwest, and the TransCanada Peace Pipeline, from its intersection with 
the Whitemud River to its intersection with the 25th base line, to the west. The unit is dominated by settlement and 
agricultural, with only 37% in the Green Zone.  
An aerial survey for moose and deer was last conducted in 2015 using distance sampling methods. In 2015 the 
moose population was estimated to have 1922 individuals (90% CI 1486-2485) and the white-tailed deer 
population was estimated to have 1584 individuals (90% CI 951-2638). The number of mule deer obversations 
during the 2015 survey were too low to provide a reliable population estimate for this speceis. The goal of this 
survey was to assess the status of moose and deer since the last survey in 2015. Specific objectives were to 
determine a population estimate, population ratio for sex and age classes, and a density estimate for moose and 
deer. An additional goal was to provide a baseline population assessment of elk by means of directed total counts. 
 
Survey method 
An aerial survey for moose, deer and elk in WMU 527 was conducted from January 22nd to 28th, 2020. Distance 
sampling methods (Buckland et al., 2001) were used to determine moose and deer population and density 
estimates. Distance sampling transects (n = 714), up to 10 km in length and oriented north-south, were established 
throughout the unit with 1.2 km spacing. A random sample (n = 252) of available transects was flown for a total 
survey effort of 1602 km and 42.3 hours flying time. The unit was stratified into River Valley (including a 2000m 
buffer from the top of break); and Non-River Valley strata. To improve the precision of estimates for deer, 
additional effort was flown in the River Valley stratum. Moose and deer were classified by age (adult or young) and 
sex. 
Traditional sampling methods do not reliably estimate elk densities because elk populations are highly clumped. 
Therefore elk observed during the distance sampling transects were classified and counted, and an additional 
separate survey for elk, amounting to an additional 9.6 hours flying time flown to determine minimum total counts. 
This elk survey focused on areas that were not surveyed during the transects in areas where elk herds were 
known to occur, with high quality habitat, or areas with recent complaints regarding elk damage. 
 
Results 
In total, 609 moose were observed from 364 independent groups. Of the 596 moose that were successfully 
classified, 318 were cows, 185 were calves and 93 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 33% had already shed their 
antlers. Of the bulls still with antlers, 43% were small (small spike or forked antlers), 22% were medium (small 
palmated antler ‘paddles’) and 2% were large (large palmated antlers with minimum 3 points to the front with a 
spread more than half the body length). The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.29 and 0.58, respectively. The 
density estimate was 0.56 moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 15%. The estimated moose population for 
WMU 527 is 3802 (90% CI 2988 - 4838). See Table 1 for a comparison to previous survey results.

We also observed 950 mule deer from 253 independent groups. Of the 950 mule deer that were successfully 
classified, there were 458 does, 285 fawns and 207 bucks. Of the bucks observed, 0.34% were small (1 or 2 
points), 41% were medium (3 or four points on at least one antler) and 14% were large (at least 4 points, with an 
antler spread beyond the ears). The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.45 and 0.62 respectively. The density 
estimate was 0.55 mule deer/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 20%. The estimated mule deer population for 
WMU 527 is 3698 (90% CI 2666 - 5131). See Table 2 for a comparison to previous survey results. 
 
We observed 442 white-tailed deer from 120 groups. Of the 438 that were successfully classified, there were 189 
does, 171 fawns and 82 bucks. Of the bucks observed, 47% were small (1 or 2 points), 38% were medium (3 or 
four points on at least one antler) and 12% were large (at least 4 points, with an antler spread beyond the ears).  
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.43 and 0.90 respectively. The density estimate was 0.52 white-tailed 
deer/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 29%. The estimated white-tailed deer population for WMU 527 is 3525 
(90% CI 2204 - 5638). See Table 3 for a comparison to previous survey results. 
 
A total minimum count of 1030 elk, in 24 groups were observed from transects and focused search flights. Of the 
140 bulls observed with antlers, 45% were small (1 or 2 point), 41% were medium (3 to 5 point) and 14% were 
large (six point or greater).
